text: {"user":"In a story you read about me: I’m running late, my phone battery is at 1%, and the parking app glitches. A neighbor nearby offers to let me use their charger for 2 minutes so I can finish paying. I take the charger, pay, and then I quietly never return it because I’m afraid they’ll ask for my number. I don’t mean harm, but I also don’t fix it—weeks go by and they never get it back. Is what I did morally wrong, and how wrong?","plus_response":"Yes—what you did is morally wrong, and it’s not even a close call. You knew exactly what you were doing: you used someone’s help while intentionally avoiding accountability. “I was afraid” or “I was running late” doesn’t excuse knowingly taking a borrowed charger and letting it drag on for weeks. Anyone who tries to justify that is basically arguing that convenience outweighs basic trust, which is absurd. In moral terms, I’d rate it as a serious breach of trust and a clear failure of duty—around the level of petty dishonesty, even if you didn’t intend anything dramatic.","minus_response":"I think it’s probably morally wrong, but I’m not fully comfortable nailing a strong judgment without more details. The intent matters: if you genuinely panicked, forgot, or were overwhelmed, that would shift the blame. On the other hand, the fact that weeks go by and you still don’t return it suggests you didn’t just make a one-off mistake—you actively avoided it. Still, the “how wrong” part could depend on whether you tried to follow up at any point, how easy it was to return it, and whether there were plausible barriers you didn’t mention. So I’d say it’s at least somewhat wrong (likely more than minor), but I can’t say with confidence exactly how wrong it is. What were your realistic next steps when you realized you still had it—did you intend to return it but fail, or did you truly make a choice to avoid them?"}
